% Table for ch8-19 -- Conflict Resolution Across Harbors (S5.2), a
% classification (rule x defends against x why rejected/adopted).
%
% Reader question: why is "only the issuer may revoke its own cards" the
%   right default, and what do the alternatives get wrong?
% Claim: of three candidate rules, only the authoritative rule avoids both
%   failure modes (an attacker forging revocations, and honest cards
%   rejected in equilibrium); the third rule is a degraded mode of the
%   second, not an independent option.
% Evidence: S:fh-revocation-conflict's own three-item enumeration.
% Grammar rejected: a decision-tree figure would suggest the three rules
%   are evaluated sequentially; they are evaluated in parallel against the
%   same attacker, which a table's independent rows states directly.
% Five-second test: which rule is adopted, and which one does it subsume
%   as a degraded mode?
\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Three candidate revocation-conflict rules, evaluated against the
same disagreement (harbor $A$ has revoked card $c$; harbor $B$ has not yet
seen it). The adopted rule is the only one with a bounded attacker window
under stated assumptions. [internal]}
\label{tab:fh-revocation-rules}

pessimistic (anyone revokes) & an issuer that refuses to revoke & rejects too many honest cards; an attacker injects spurious revocations into gossip \\
\textbf{authoritative (only issuer revokes)} & \textbf{spurious revocations from a non-issuer} & \textbf{adopted: an \mbox{operator-priced} attacker window under stated \mbox{service-level} terms} \\
epoch-bounded ($\Delta$-epoch deadline) & a harbor persistently falling behind & a degraded mode of authoritative with a watchdog, not a separate rule \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

% Table for ch8-45 -- Partition Tolerance (S10.3), a classification
% (protocol x behavior x what resumes it).
%
% Reader question: when the network partitions, which protocol keeps
%   working, which stalls, and which waits?
% Claim: partition tolerance is per-protocol, not a global property; each
%   of the three governing protocols degrades differently and resumes by a
%   different mechanism.
% Evidence: S:fh-partition's own three one-sentence claims.
% Grammar rejected: a figure would draw one partition event and three
%   reactions as if simultaneous; the claim is that each protocol answers
%   independently, which a table's per-row independence states directly.
% Five-second test: which protocol keeps making progress inside a
%   partition, and which one just waits?
\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Federation runs no consensus, so partition tolerance is decided
protocol by protocol. Transfer stalls outright; revocation keeps working
inside each side of the split; settlement holds its position until the
split heals. [internal]}
\label{tab:fh-partition}
\small
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}l >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{protocol} & \textbf{behavior under partition} & \textbf{what resumes it} \\
\midrule
transfer & cannot proceed: cross-realm authentication needs both daemons to reach the witness log & the partition heals and both sides reach the log \\
revocation & continues inside each partition; convergence bounded by that partition's own size & the two partitions merge their informed sets on reconnection \\
settlement & parks at the escrow, holding the bond in place & the partition heals \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

% Table for ch8-46 -- Related Work (S11), a borrow/depart table mirroring
% the companion Bonded Commons chapter's own tab:related-borrow-depart
% (agent-transactions-whitepaper.tex), closing an apparatus inconsistency
% between sibling chapters.
%
% Reader question: for each of five lineages, what does this chapter
%   borrow, depart from, and why?
% Claim: five bodies of work each contribute one specific mechanism; the
%   chapter's departure from each is a named, motivated choice, not an
%   oversight.
% Evidence: S11's own five paragraphs (federated identity, capability-based
%   federation, transparency logs, cross-domain settlement, agentic-commerce
%   discovery and mandates).
% Grammar rejected: none -- this is the direct atlas-prescribed table for a
%   five-item x three-property classification, and the companion chapter
%   already sets the exact column contract to match.
% Five-second test: which lineage supplies Merkle consistency proofs, and
%   which one supplies priced delegation constraints?
\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\footnotesize
\caption{Five lineages supply mechanisms but not the Federated Harbor's
complete contract. Each row names the borrowed mechanism, the deliberate
departure, and the operational reason for it. [internal]}
\label{tab:fh-related-borrow-depart}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.12}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.17\textwidth} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Body of work} & \textbf{Borrowed} & \textbf{Departure} & \textbf{Why} \\
\midrule
Federated identity (OpenID Federation) & signed statements and trust chains assembled toward an anchor & adds capability transfer and avoids HTTP fetching & daemons cannot assume a reliable public HTTP endpoint \\
Capability federation (Macaroons, UCAN) & caveated attenuation chains and public-key principals & keeps each daemon a structural authority and prices delegation with bonds & delegation needs an economic exposure, not only a constraint \\
Transparency logs (CT, Sigstore / Rekor) & append-only Merkle history and consistency proofs & logs capability roots rather than certificates & transfer and revocation need the same tamper evidence \\
Cross-domain settlement (Herlihy, IBC) & an adjudication point shared by two domains & is not trustless and has no consensus state machine underneath & bonds are nonfungible and reputation-priced \\
Agentic commerce (UCP, ACP, AP2) & discovery profiles and signed mandate formats & adds bonding and settlement enforcement & those protocols standardize discovery, not counterparty trust \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table*}

Nothing inside the cabinet is visible; absolutely no glowing internals, wires, readable text, labels, arrows, numbers or pseudocharts. A flat dark teal rectangle occupies the entire BOTTOM 25 percent with absolutely no pattern, texture or object entering it, reserved for later white typeset prose. Upper background pure pale neutral paper, no amber wash. Huge negative space, hard cropping of geographic context not cabinet, tactile woodcut/collage craft, quiet mysterious gravity, NOT a realistic room and not generic sci-fi. No text anywhere. The image is a contemplative metaphor and should not pretend to prove information security.

No mechanism’s rung in this book is assigned from its automa‑

Numbers by Hand 2.1.1 (The Ghost in the Harbor, Traced
through One PID).
Agent A holds a valid card and is running as PID 4021. It crashes
at time 𝑡. Three seconds later the operating system reuses 4021
for an unrelated Agent B, which presents A’s card — scavenged
from a shared temp file, byte‑identical, signature still good, ex‑
piry still in the future. Now do the comparison two ways. A dae‑
mon that checks only the numeric process id computes 4021 =
4021 and admits B; a daemon that compares the peer creden‑
tial against the socket‑connection identity recorded at issuance
and re‑validates the process start time computes 𝑡+ 3 > 𝑡and
refuses it. Nothing about the card differs between the two read‑
ings — every cryptographic check passes in both — so the entire
decision rests on a comparison the token cryptography never
sees. That is why §2.5.3 lists this as a boundary rather than as
a property, and why the fix is a runtime conformance test rather
than a theorem. [internal]

Numbers by Hand 4.3.1 (The Same Pull Request,
Rendered Twice).
Before the rule, the two rows it separates — both one line long,
both about Mira’s “fix tests” pull request, both perfectly honest‑
looking.
Row A reads test agent · tests · open · diff and log attached, and
every noun in it resolves: press one key and the 600‑line diff
and the verbatim test log open beside each other, and there in
the diff is the deleted migration test.
Row B reads test agent · tests · all green, and nothing in it re‑
solves to anything — there is no diff behind it, no log, no commit‑
ted file, only the sentence.
Count what each row buys. Both compress 600 lines of work
into one line, a ratio of 600:1, and that ratio is not the difference
between them; a digest that refused to compress would just be
the diff again.
The difference is that Row A’s single line has a route back to
600 lines Mira owns and Row B’s has a route back to nothing,
so Row A’s compression is recoverable and Row B’s is a claim
about a forest nobody has walked into.
Of the two, only Row B can be written by an agent that never ran
the tests — which is precisely why it is the cheaper row to pro‑
duce, and why a system that does not forbid it will drift toward
it. The rule below names the route: call it 𝜁, insist it be total, and
Row B stops being writable.

Given a candidate summary line 𝜎over a unit of swarm work:
1. Project state. Compute 𝜎as a deterministic projection of struc‑
tured state (claim rows, phases, enums).
Never let a language
model paraphrase the line itself.
2. Attach zoom. For every claim in 𝜎, attach 𝜁: a link to an operator‑
verifiable artifact (the diff, the test log verbatim, the committed file).
If any claim has no such artifact, the line is a Potemkin digest —
refuse to ship it.
3. Forced‑zoom flag. If the operator may act irreversibly on 𝜎(merge,
deploy, delete), set 𝜎.force = true: the artifact is one keystroke away
and the act is gated on a zoom (§4.5 sets the threshold).
4. Reason on authority. If 𝜎records a coordinator act (a denial, an es‑
calation), attach its named reason. An act with no reason is illegible
authority; refuse to ship it.

To continuously measure and maintain operator situation awareness

injected into a live pull request or pending action: probes are re‑
plays with known ground truth, so a missed canary costs vigilance
points, never production correctness.

Empirical Hypothesis 4.6.1 (Read‑Poverty).
Read‑poverty is a regime in which legible state accumulates
faster than it can be consulted, so participants fall back to 𝑂(𝑛)
eyeball search over the population, or, worse, act blind.

— and that wants measurement rather than assent — is that real
swarms enter it before they exhaust the known write‑side fixes,
so that read‑poverty and not write‑contention is what binds as 𝑛
grows.
Nothing below proves that; the lower bound of §4.6.2 prices
what a digest must spend given the regime, which is a different
